Then you move to Blue group (level 3) - this is the group where people start leaving. The rides are more difficult, the expectations are higher but the pay remains the same. If you stay long enough, you get to move to Red group (level 4). Again, the rides are more difficult, more safety issues and risks & more responsibility but the pay STAYS THE SAME (minimum pay). Recently, it's become more difficult to work within McDonald's, mainly due to their decisions to run more promotions, and to create unrealistic goals for the crew. It's becoming far too difficult for McDonald's employees to do their jobs, with constant introduction of new promotional items and products, and with this new kind of focus in some smaller stores to reduce the cost of labour. The stores have become frequently understaffed, the crew are expected to work even harder in a bid to keep up with the new gourmet range (with the same mimimum wage pay). In previous years, it was easy to progress within your own store; now, not so much. The process of progression can take months within individual stores, with management overlooking those loyal, hard working senior crew, to prioritise the younger crew who receive more shifts throughout the week. Review Text: Most of the time, while working as a customer service supervisor, we were understaffed. Team members from other departments were supposed to help out during busy periods, but rarely did, which left customers complaining about ques and service quality as there was a rush to get customers out of the store. Service staff got tired of being stuck on register and often complained or regularly called in sick and cancelled shifts at the last minute, making these shifts very difficult to replace. A number of jobs were required of service staff in addition to customer service (for example cleaning, putting stock away, filling drink fridges and confectionery stands) and due to lack of staff these jobs were often left not done. Store managers and other higher up staff would then complain to me and my direct customer service manager, without recognizing that the reason tasks were not completed was due to lack of staff, not incompetence. Customers, particularly cigarette customers and refund customers tended to be difficult. Cigarette customers were often rude and demanding, as were refund customers. Some refund customers claimed to know our refund policy more than myself, who had been working there for over 7 years, and demanded free products, when this was not allowed.

If you’re a store manager at Aldi, forget about work-life balance. You’ll be the last one to get it. All those work-life balance rules? They’re mostly just for show. The pay is decent, but it can feel like you’re selling your soul to the Devil. Sure, you’ll have money, but you might end up sacrificing your physical and mental health. Burnout is right around the corner, especially with crazy goals and not enough staff. You’ll find yourself doing the work of four people. Directors and area managers have no clue what it’s really like in the stores. Honestly, they should try being a store manager for three months—I bet they wouldn’t last a month, even as a store assistant. And those yearly store manager conferences? Just a horror show. It’s like a competition to see who can be the most self-absorbed. Everyone acts like they’re on a talk show, but it really feels more like an episode of "The Office," with everyone channeling their inner Michael Scott. It’s just a bunch of kids in suits pretending to be important. They could easily turn those conferences into an email, and the money spent on them could be better used to support the stores or reward the staff—anything but boosting their own egos. Hearing “without you, we are nothing” feels empty when they’re at home dreaming up more ways to pile on the pressure for those of us who are working hard. They schedule important tasks like remerch on payroll days, which is just ridiculous. Choose easy days—Wednesdays and Thursdays—when there are no specials or payroll to worry about. The distribution center is already a mess, and things that should be simple turn into chaos. What’s really missing is a more human touch—actually caring about people. We’re not robots, but it seems like the company doesn’t really care about store workers. It’s all just a cover in the contract; they’re mainly focused on making money while those who genuinely care are struggling with their health. You’re replaceable, no matter how good you are, because the ones who really get ahead are usually the favorites. We all know how that goes, right? So if you value your health, this job might not be for you.

Management values saving money far, far more than they value good workers. • Understaffed: This goes for pretty much every retail environment, but is especially true here. Lack of staff paired with all of the other things wrong with this workplace means that you are pretty much set up for failure every single day. One challenge I’ve noticed at ALPA is that remote staff can sometimes feel a real sense of isolation or disconnect from the wider community, especially in days when in-person energy is high. It’s genuinely difficult at times for remote team members to feel the same level of belonging and real-time camaraderie as those on-site. While we do a lot to bridge that gap and offer support—and I know we’re always here to help—it’s something that still needs attention. That said, recognizing this is what pushes us to keep finding new ways to include everyone, strengthen connections, and make sure every voice feels truly heard and valued, wherever they’re working from.

ALPA operates in a fast-paced, challenging environment. Those working remote need to work with challenges of limited resources, a different cultural context, surviving away from family, and problem-solving unexpected situations.

The complexity of operating across such a wide range of sectors and regions—from remote Northern Territory communities to Far North Queensland—can sometimes make it difficult to maintain consistent service delivery, cultural sensitivity, and community engagement. Balancing commercial success with social responsibility is no small feat, and there’s always a risk that some communities might feel underserved or disconnected if communication and feedback loops aren’t strong. That said, this isn’t a criticism of ALPA’s intentions—it’s more a reflection of the natural challenges that come with scaling up while staying true to grassroots values.

Working as IT support at the Arnhem Land Progress Aboriginal Corporation presents unique challenges, shaped by its remote locations and community-focused mission. One major difficulty is maintaining reliable internet and network infrastructure across isolated areas, where outages and limited connectivity can disrupt services. Delivering and setting up hardware in these regions also takes extra time and planning. Supporting a diverse workforce, many of whom may have limited experience with technology, requires clear and patient communication, as well as culturally sensitive training. You often need to troubleshoot a wide range of issues, from printers and laptops to network systems, sometimes without immediate access to advanced tools or backup. Balancing these technical demands with ALPA’s commitment to empowering Indigenous communities means your role isn’t just about fixing problems, it’s about enabling people, services, and businesses to thrive.

This created a demanding work environment as staff were asked to undertake tasks and responsibilities well-outside their roles to make-up for the lack of numbers (i.e. a Site Foreman, a Safety Officer, a Site Engineer / Cadet, etc.). With regards to contract administration and design coordination, I personally felt that there was a lot of unnecessary risk taken on from a Head Contractor. Additionally, through my experiences on the project, communicating, coordinating and receiving information from our own suppliers in China for prefabricated structural and façade elements was beyond difficult (much easier to deal with external subcontractors). Between supervising works on-site & day-to-day site tasks and the coordination & administration side of things in the office, an 80-hour minimum working week is the norm here (6 days a week mandatory). This realistically cannot be sustained. The main reason I decided to resign was the way the company handled the coronavirus pandemic back in mid-March 2020 - half the team was placed on standby for approximately 3 months and additionally there was a freeze on hiring much needed site staff.
